Pack. Scan. Send.

No container nearby? The bag goes back with your next return.

  1. Pack

    Clothes and shoes you no longer wear. Clean and dry; holes and tears are fine.

  2. Scan

    Scan the code on the cap with the app or your phone camera. Then the bag is yours.

  3. Send

    With your next return, on its own with your shop's return label, or at the checkout in a store.

  4. Get your voucher

    It comes at the carrier's first scan. Loops and the donation follow once the bag is weighed.

By 17 April 2028 every EU country must have extended producer responsibility (EPR) for textiles in place. Germany has published key points; the law hasn't been passed yet.

Questions, answered.

Does it cost anything?

No. The bag, the app and registering cost nothing. If you send the bag on its own, your shop's return terms apply.

How do I get a tcycled bag?

Ask for one when you order from a partner shop, at the checkout or in the app, and it comes in your parcel. No bag yet? Use your own box with a label from the app.

Do I need the app?

No. Register the bag on this page with your email, and the voucher comes by email. The app shows every step and keeps all your vouchers in one wallet.

What is my voucher worth?

Your shop sets the value and the conditions. You see both as soon as the bag is registered, before you send it.

When do I get my voucher?

As soon as the carrier scans your bag for the first time, or when store staff scan the cap. Usually that's the day you send it.

My clothes have holes. Can I still send them?

Yes, as long as they're clean and dry. What can't be worn again is recycled where possible; what can't be recycled goes to energy recovery. Dirty things belong in the household bin.

Can I send shoes?

Yes, tied together in pairs. A single shoe can't be worn again, so please keep those out.

Where do my clothes go?

To Artus in Bad Oldesloe, where every bag is weighed and sorted by hand. See what happens next.

What are Loops?

You get 1 Loop for every bag that arrives. Spend three Loops for €5 off a product made with recycled fibre.

Sorting

We look at every piece.

Artus weighs every bag in Bad Oldesloe and sorts it by hand. Each piece goes where it is still most useful: reuse first, then recycling, energy last. We show you the split.

The journey In this order Follow a piece Product passport How we count

From your hallway to its next owner.

  1. Your hallwayYou fill the bag and scan the cap.
  2. On its wayThe carrier's first scan unlocks your voucher.
  3. WeighedArtus weighs the bag in Bad Oldesloe. Loops and the donation follow.
  4. Sorted by handTrained sorters pick the best next use for every piece.
  5. Next useWorn again or recycled. Only what can't be used any more goes to energy recovery.

In this order. Always.

Reuse comes first: a piece worn again can stand in for a new one. Recycling comes next. Energy recovery is for what can't be used any other way.

ReuseWorn again as second-hand

Pieces that can be worn again are sold as second-hand clothing.

It's the best outcome: the water and energy that went into making them have already been spent, and the piece keeps using them.

RefashionRepaired or remade by partner workshops

A broken zip, a missing button or a small tear can send a piece to a partner workshop.

There it can be repaired, or remade into something new, like a bag or a patchwork jacket.

New fibreRecycled into fibre for new clothes

Worn-out pieces of suitable material can be shredded and spun into new yarn.

How much of it ends up in new clothes, we show in the split.

Other productsInsulation, cleaning cloths, filling

Fibre that can't become clothing again becomes insulation, cleaning cloths or filling.

It replaces new material in products that last for years.

Energy recoveryFor what can't be used any other way

What can't be reused or recycled, like wet, mouldy or heavily mixed material, is used to make energy.

That's why we ask for clean, dry clothes: it keeps this tier as small as possible.

Follow a piece.

Pick something from your wardrobe and see where it could go next. These are possible routes, not a promise for every piece.

Your old jeans

Denim is tough. Jeans that arrive whole usually still fit someone.

  • ReuseIf they still fit someone, they're sold as second-hand.
  • RefashionA broken zip or a torn knee goes to a partner workshop.
  • New fibreWorn thin, the cotton can be spun into new yarn.

Your sneakers

Tied together in pairs, shoes can be worn again. A single shoe can't.

  • ReuseWith life left in the sole, they're checked, cleaned and sold second-hand.
  • Other productsWorn out, their rubber and textile can become new materials.

Your favourite hoodie

It was there for everything. Now it can be there for someone else.

  • ReuseSoft, warm and whole: straight to second-hand.
  • RefashionHoles in the cuffs are patched by a partner workshop.
  • New fibreToo far gone? The cotton blend can be recycled into new fibre.

A party dress

Worn twice, photographed once. It still has Saturdays ahead.

  • ReuseSold second-hand to someone with a party coming up.
  • RefashionA loose seam or a missing sequin gets fixed first.

A worn-out T-shirt

Faded, stretched and a little see-through. Still useful.

  • New fibreClean cotton can be spun into new yarn.
  • Other productsMixed fibres become cleaning cloths or insulation.
  • Energy recoveryIf it can't be reused or recycled.

How we count.

Weighed, not guessed

Every bag is weighed when it arrives. Your figures start from your own kilos, not an average bag.

No number without a source

Water and CO₂e are only shown for the reused share, with the published study they come from right next to the number. Until a source has been checked, we show none.

Rounded and dated

We round, and we say which period a figure covers.

Abroad included

We publish how much is sold as second-hand outside Germany, and where it goes.

For brands

Take-back you can prove.

tcycled takes your customers' clothes back, by post and in your stores. Artus sorts them by hand in Bad Oldesloe, and artusNet records what happens to every kilo, from the first scan to where it goes next.

Data through artusNet

Groundwork for product passports

artusNet stores the origin data that digital product passports for textiles can build on, once the EU rules are set.

Two parts, kept apart.

tcycled runs the take-back: bags, scans, vouchers and carriers. artusNet is the data layer between your systems and Artus's SAP: weights, outcomes and the chain of custody.

The rules are coming in steps.

What is already in force, and what Germany is still deciding. tcycled records the weights and outcomes from the first bag on.

Today
  1. 1 Jan 2025Separate collectionEU countries must collect textiles separately from other waste.
  2. 16 Oct 2025Textile EPR becomes EU lawThe revised Waste Framework Directive enters into force.
  3. 27 Mar 2026Key points for GermanyThe environment ministry proposes competing producer schemes and a 70% collection target.
  4. 19 Jul 2026No destroying unsold clothesThe ESPR ban applies to large companies, returns included.
  5. 2 Mar 2027One reporting formatDiscarded unsold products are reported in a standard EU format.
  6. 17 Jun 2027National law dueMember states must have transposed the directive.
  7. 17 Apr 2028EPR in every member stateProducers pay for collecting and sorting the textiles they sell.
  8. 19 Jul 2030Medium-sized companies tooThe destruction ban extends to medium-sized companies.

Sources: EUWID European Commission BMUKN key points Trustrace VdA

One API for the take-back.

Add bags to orders, accept them at the till and hear about every step. Weights and outcomes come through artusNet.

  • POST /v1/bag-requestsAdd a tcycled bag to a customer's order.
  • POST /v1/own-box-labelsCreate a label for a customer's own box.
  • POST /v1/store-dropoffsAccept a bag at your checkout and issue the voucher.
  • GET /v1/bags/{code}Public bag status for your site and your app.
  • return.in_transit, dropoff.accepted, return.weighedWebhooks for your CRM, checkout and reporting.

Draft. Endpoints may change before launch.

The mark is a t that loops back.

A lowercase t whose tail swings round into a recycling arrow. The wordmark is always lowercase, and the endorsement reads "by artus".
